newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FEATURE - Kazakhstan seeks real stock market by year-end.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Kazakhstan seeks real stock market by year-end.

text.p: Resource-rich Kazakhstan, looking for foreign investment to end its economic slump, plans to open a fully functioning stock exchange this year and has charged a former senior central banker with carrying out the task.
"My personal task is to set up a viable stock market, because investors usually look at a country's stock index before putting money in its economy," Grigory Marchenko told Reuters.

Marchenko, 37, a fluent English speaker who used to be deputy central bank chairman, was appointed to head the National Securities Market Commission last November. He said the market was essential to make his job worthwhile.

"I hope in the next six months the necessary stock market infrastructure will be formed," Marchenko said. "It is unacceptable for me to be in charge of the securities market commission when this market does not exist."
Marchenko said his ambitious plans were backed by President Nursultan Nazarbayev, to whom the commission would eventually report directly.
"BLUE CHIPS" TO BE FLOATED ON NEW EXCHANGE

Marchenko's plan is to set up "a full-fledged stock exchange with necessary listing procedures" and attract foreign capital to the former Soviet republic by offering shares in a number of large and stable "blue chip" companies.

The new exchange, which has not yet been named, will eventually trade shares in 56 large companies, all of them selected for their potential ability to attract outside investors. The initial plans are more modest.
"I think we could start with trading shares in 10 or 15 of these companies," Marchenko said.

He said shares in the companies, many of them involved in extracting and processing Kazakhstan's abundant natural resources, would go like hot cakes if the firms presented financial figures to international accounting standards, audited by respectable Western firms.
"In the next two years the bulk of investment on our market will come from abroad... For this we need to achieve maximum transparency of the market," Marchenko said.

The government, working with the World Bank's private-sector affiliate, the International Financial Corporation, and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, plans an international seminar in June to allow heads of the future "blue chips" to meet potential investors.
STRATEGIC AS WELL AS PORTFOLIO INVESTORS SOUGHT

Marchenko did not rule out the possibility that controlling stakes of 51-60 percent in some companies could be first sold to strategic investors and the remaining shares would later be sold to portfolio investors on the stock exchange.
"This is not bad, especially if the controlling stakes are bought by serious investors -- a good signal for portfolio ones," he said.
He said portfolio investors could bring up to $300 million into the former Soviet republic this year, after the stock market starts up.
The new stock exchange will be formed from two existing exchanges which won a government tender last December for the right to sell government-owned shares.
The loser of the tender was the Central Asian Stock Exchange (CASE), set up in December 1994 and faltering ever since.
Volumes on CASE have been low and its management concedes that it can hardly be described as a stock exchange "due to the absence of necessary stock market infrastructure".
The authorities are already working to remedy this shortfall and the government has asked the central bank and the Kazakh Stock Exchange to set up a central depository of securities.
It will be linked both to the stock exchange and to brokers' and dealers' back offices and will be compatible with international standards.
WORK ON BOURSE INFRASTRUCTURE ALREADY UNDER WAY
Parliament is discussing how bills which can be traded on the securities market can be issued and how best to create investment funds and register securities deals.
And some 90 local broker and dealer companies have been given three months to boost their capital to at least $130,000 from the present-day $20,000.
Marchenko said the final goal was to raise the capital of brokers and dealers to $1 million "to attract serious foreign investors".
His commission is also planning to create a nationwide system of independent registrars.

Marchenko said all the necessary stock market infrastructure could be created by July or August, a strong signal for foreign investors eyeing Kazakhstan's huge oil and gas sectors, as well as energy and communications companies.
He said he was also keen to attract small investors.

The government plans to transform privatisation funds, which mushroomed when 1,768 companies were privatised for coupons issued free of charge in 1994-95 to every Kazakh citizen, into Western-style mutual funds and investment companies, but it is not yet clear how the transformation will work.
